catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, section 2.2.7 Tone, pp. 63-64 = chapter-2 pp. 50-51 (p. 63 viewed); section 2.2.7.1 Tone Sequence, p. 65; section 2.0 General, p. 14. Secondary: Kosha 1986, pp. 107-108.
catalog_quote: Tone is the height of pitch and change of pitch which is associated with the pronunciation of syllable or words and which affects the meaning of the word by level or by falling. ... Moyon has also the tonal system in the sense that pitch variation affects the meaning of the word by level or by falling etc. There are two tones in Moyon. They are level and falling tone. The falling tone is marked by (\) and level tone is unmarked. The two tones are constrasted in minimal sets given below. ... [p. 65] There are four tone sequence in Moyon within a word. They are (i) level + level, (ii) fall + fall (iii) fall + level (iv) level + fall. ... [p. 14] Tones are suprasegmental phonemes. In Moyon language, there are twentynine segmental phonemes and two suprasegmental phonemes.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (53 pp., ABBYY text). Printed page numbers sit at the top of each page; printed p. 63 = PDF page 50, which carries section "2.2.7. Tone". The quoted sentences ("Moyon has also the tonal system in the sense that pitch variation affects the meaning of the word by level or by falling etc. There are two tones in Moyon. They are level and falling tone. The falling tone is marked by (\) and level tone is unmarked. The two tones are constrasted in minimal sets given below.") are there word for word, including the "constrasted" typo; the quote only elides a paragraph break after "etc." Section 2.2.7.1 "Tone Sequence" (four sequences: level+level, fall+fall, fall+level, level+fall, "within a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The grammar treats Moyon as a two-tone language (level vs falling, with four permitted tone sequences in disyllables) and says nothing at all about word stress or accent; the only 'suprasegmental phonemes' recognised are the two tones. The older two-page note by Kosha (1986: 107-108) likewise calls Moyon tonal (three tones there) and mentions 'a change of tone or stress in a word' only as an aside about expressive pitch on the final syllable, not as a rule of stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Sources disagree on the tone inventory: Kongkham 2010 two tones (level, falling); Kosha 1986 three tones (high rising, low, high level).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone; tone sequences stated 'within a word' (disyllabic examples, p. 65). Data from Komlathabi village speakers (Kongkham 2010: 11).
new_statements.identity_note: Kongkham 2010 describes the Moyon of Komlathabi village, Chandel district, Manipur (three informants aged 25-65); no dialects are distinguished, so this is moyo1238 itself. Kosha 1986 gives no village. Both sources call the language Moyon (Naga); autonym Bujur/Bujuur.

sources.note: Two-page note: 'Like the other neighbouring Tibeto-Burman languages, Moyon is also a tonal language. A word can have different meanings with different tones, which are three in number' (high rising, low, high level; p. 107). Only mention of stress is a passing aside: 'Similarly a change of tone or stress in a word, can give different shades of meaning with different degrees of feeling', illustrated with pitch changes on the last syllable of [inunseve] 'it was enjoyable' (pp. 107-108).
